subsubtopic: ACCOUNTABILITY TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last week the Liberal Cabinet dished out another $250 million of public funds to Canadair to continue its money losing fiasco. The Cabinet did not think that this transaction required parliamentary approval. This is one example, of many, of the failure of parliamentary accountability and thus the failure of democracy. Crown corporations for too long have escaped public and parliamentary scrutiny.
To correct this the Liberals have brought in Bill C-153, which 1 can only describe as feeble. The Bill does not provide for comprehensive audits and fails to improve in any substantial way the accountability of Crown corporations to Parliament.
Crown corporations must be made accountable to Parliament. Burgeoning sub-government must be controlled. In the first place, all audits should be done by the Auditor General and not by some external auditing firm. Second, the competitiveness of Crown corporations should not be enhanced by public funds. Any and all public funds allotted to Crown corporations should be detailed in the budget and then thoroughly examined by a parliamentary Committee.
The accountability of Crown corporations should not stop at the Cabinet level. Crown corporations should be made accountable to the people through the Parliament of Canada.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES PLANS FOR PHASED DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, earlier this week I and two other Members of this House, and two from the Manitoba legislature, travelled to Washington to meet with a number of Members of both Houses of the American Congress to inform them of Manitoba's concerns about the proposed Garrison Diversion Unit. These types of meetings are very good and will go a long way to ensuring that Manitoba's waterways are protected from the negative aspects of the current design of the Garrison Diversion Unit.
The bottom line, Madam Speaker, is that the Garrison Diversion Unit must be redesigned to remove any transboundary transfer of water.
A new wrinkle is that the U.S. Interior Department is now proposing a phased program. It maintains that in Phase I nothing would be constructed that would adversely affect Manitoba, but Phase I includes the Lonetree Reservoir which is on the Hudson Bay side of the Continental Divide.
Even more alarming is that Interior is now proposing that the fish screens proposed for the McClusky Canal not be built, thus allowing foreign biota clear sailing across the Divide. I would point out that the International Joint Commission found the screens to be an uncertain protection against the biota transfer. Now to propose no protection at all is especially alarming. Perhaps Interior is hoping this threat will scare us into accepting these screens, flawed as they may be. Manitoba's bottom line, I repeat, is that Garrison must be redesigned so as to prevent any and all biota transfer.

subsubtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF RHOSP FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in his April budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) proposed an additional economic stimulus whereby individuals would be permitted a tax-free withdrawal of part or all of their accumulated savings in RHOSPs for the purchase of new home furnishings and appliances. This special short-term consumer incentive was intended to spur the sale of furnishings and appliances which Canadians have delayed purchasing as a result of the uncertainty caused by the recession. In the budget papers the commencement date of this proposal was stated as being April 19. However, several of my constituents have complained that when they have gone to their bank or trust company to make their RHOSP withdrawal for the purchase of furnishings and appliances, their request for the withdrawal has been denied.
The denial of these RHOSP withdrawals affects not only individuals wishing to purchase home furnishings and appliances but also affects the sales of manufacturers such as Cameo Limited, which is located in my riding of Hamilton West. I would therefore strongly urge the Minister of Finance

subsubtopic: EXPENSE EXEMPTIONS SOUGHT FOR VOLUNTARY FIREMEN AND NON-PAID COUNCILLORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is high time that the Canadian Government recognized the contribution being made by volunteers like firemen who work without remuneration, and councillors who work without pay. Provisions for exemption from income tax now for such councillors is one-third of the general expense allowance. Firemen who work without wages receive no consideration whatsoever, even though they work for the good of the community.
I recommend that consideration be included in the Act for income tax purposes for such volunteer firemen who ruin their clothes and give their time, et cetera, in fighting fires in an
amount of the average claimed by firemen who do accept wages and qualify for expense exemption. I also recommend that where councillors and mayors receive a sum of money in lieu of wages to cover costs attending meetings, travelling, checking hydrants, checking buildings, checking complaints, checking wild dogs, et cetera, this be acknowledged and accepted in the amount approved by their councils. MPs, MLAs, and MNAs all receive an expense allowance exemption from income tax, and Canadians who give their time freely, without pay, warrant consideration.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BILL BE DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, according to news reports last evening, the Conservatives and Liberals are back together again discussing ways and means of doing away with the Crow rate. Parliament and the country know nothing of what is going on, what items are now negotiable, what new policy changes are under consideration. The only thing that is consistent in this process is the apparent support of both of the old Parties for the killing of the Crow.
This House has been asked to pass a Bill, Bill C-155, that is not yet complete. By the Minister's own statements there is more to come. He says he has important amendments to make to the Bill, yet we are being asked, in effect, to buy a pig in a poke. We are asked to hear witnesses' opinions at committee stage prior to the introduction of the amendments to the Bill, because amendments come after the evidence of witnesses. This process is totally unacceptable.
I call on the Progressive Conservatives to reconsider the cozy relationship they continue and insist upon maintaining with the Liberals on this issue, in order that all of the proposals can be placed in the legislation before us. For that to happen it is vital that the current Bill C-155 be withdrawn to be broken into three separate Bills, so we can deal with each of the three separate policy items in a full, proper, and a public manner.

subsubtopic: WILLIAMSBURG SUMMIT-EFFECT ON AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY OF MINISTER'S PROPOSAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs arises out of my concern over his statements in the newspapers this week regarding free trade which he will promote and propose at the Summit meeting in Williamsburg. This is the same week that the task force report on the automotive industry was read and reviewed by everyone in the House. It was very important because it was written by employers of a large number of people in the country, and by union leaders who represent a large group. Could the Minister explain what might happen to the automobile industry if he proceeds with the free trade proposal which he is taking to Williamsburg?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WILLIAMSBURG SUMMIT-EFFECT ON AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY OF MINISTER'S PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should explain to the Hon. Member that last November at the GATT ministerial meeting the Ministers present all undertook to resist further protectionist measures. That undertaking was made by all contracting parties to the GATT. Just recently the OECD ministerial meeting not only agreed to refrain from new protectionist measures but also agreed to dismantle, as recovery proceeded, protectionist measures now in effect. Those are commitments which have already been made by member countries. Unfortunately the record of performance is not as sterling as the commitments themselves.
It would seem to me, if the summit at Williamsburg is to have credibility, that commitments with respect to antiprotectionism ought to be conducted in a meaningful environment. For that reason I have explored with my colleagues the possibility of having some way by which members of the Summit could examine the conduct in light of the commitments that have already been made, and will undoubtedly be repeated at Williamsburg. What I am stating is not a new commitment made by any government, but commitments that will appear more credible in the eyes of the public at the present time.

APPLICATION OF IMPORT QUOTA SYSTEM TO TEXTILES AND CLOTHING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the same Minister. I do not necessarily accept all the arguments he makes with regard to protectionism and what flows from the GATT negotiations.
It troubles me when the Minister says we do not want to enlarge on any protectionist measure. I would ask him to be a little more definitive. For example, as the Minister knows, we have quotas on imports of textiles. That has been the measure of protection which we have offered that particular industry in Canada. Would the maintenance or expansion of either the quota within that industry, or other quotas, in his view be offensive or be a breach of the GATT negotiations and the intent thereof? In other words, when he says we do not want to enlarge our protectionist measures, would the quota system for imported products such as textiles offend that particular principle, in his view?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPLICATION OF IMPORT QUOTA SYSTEM TO TEXTILES AND CLOTHING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member realizes that even with the GATT negotiations themselves, which were finally ratified by the Government of which the Hon. Member was a member, textiles certainly had a special status, and that the industrialized countries, including Canada, the United States and the European Community, have had to take measures to protect their domestic industries against very strong competition, particularly from the developing world.
In my reply to the Hon. Member who began the Question Period, I drew a distinction between additional protectionist measures and dismantling existing protectionist measures. It is the former that I had mainly in mind with respect to the Williamsburg Summit.

Madam Speaker, I am not sure the Minister has answered my question, but let me go on. If we proceed either to dismantling or to no further protectionist measures, we run the risk within certain industries, particularly consumer goods-I have already mentioned textiles; I also think immediately of furniture manufacturing, and I am sure the Minister's colleague responsible for energy would be very informed of this, coming from the riding he does-the risk or peril in which we put a large number of Canadian workers.
I would be much more comfortable about Williamsburg if I knew that within the Government of which the Minister forms
a part there was a strategy for protecting or providing alternative employment for large groups of Canadians within various manufacturing sectors, particularly in central Canada. I see no sign of that, so is the Government going to Williamsburg, as the Minister has said, with respect to this anti-protectionism and the implementation of GATT agreement, without any alternative long range strategy for dealing with a situation that could very well create, as I think the Minister would agree, potentially large groups of displaced workers within the various manufacturing sectors in central Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, I do not agree at all that what is being proposed leads to the displacement of large numbers of manufacturing jobs. I think that to draw a conclusion like that from what I have been saying is very unjustified. What I have been saying is that it is a very simple proposition. If we intend to nurture the recovery that is now beginning, one of the most solid ways of doing it for Canada and for other countries is to ensure that markets are kept open and that there is the possibility for Canadian exporters to sell in other markets. This is in our interests as a country because of our dependence on foreign trade and because of the large proportion of our Gross National Product that derives from foreign trade. It is in our interests to ensure that markets are kept open to the greatest possible extent.
It seems to me that it would be a great mistake for industrialized countries, having gone through the worst part of the recession and having, in my view, resisted protectionist measures to a great extent, to slide into protectionism now that the recovery is beginning. I believe that that would hinder the recovery and hinder the growth of jobs in Canada and in other countries. That is the point of view which I will be expressing at Williamsburg along with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment first of all, and I believe it is the general opinion of my fellow Members from the Province of Alberta, on the high quality of the Commission's work. I think that this time, we are generally satisfied with the commissioners' proposals, and it is certainly the best report we have had on electoral redistribution in the Province of Alberta.

1 know the commissioners. I may say that they have used some of the political sense that we hope all commissioners have. One of the great difficulties in the past has been that
those who know their constituencies best, the Members, were the least listened to concerning their knowledge of such factors as ease of communication, general representation, cohesiveness and interest in the community. These are all factors which I, and I believe the majority of Members, deem far more important than just the mere numbers indicated in census reports, which are quite often too outdated by the time recommendations come into force in the actual field to be meaningful in the representation of the people of Canada.
At a later occasion a few incidents will be raised by some of my colleagues. 1 trust that this will not simply be a transfer of debate on this report aux calendes grecques, in other words, some six or eight months from now. 1 rather suspect, with the dilatory interest the Government has shown in matters of this kind, that it will be put off and delayed, thus making a redistribution more irrelevant as time goes on.
As I indicated, a few points will be raised in regard to one or two constituencies. It is not with that particular point that I want to deal. As far as my constituency is concerned, I am more than satisfied with the geographical distribution because the Commissioners in Alberta have finally paid attention to recommendations made by many others and myself. One former Commissioner had told me on occasion, "You have had three kicks at the cat." But he did not pay any attention. The urban communities are chosen boundaries that are well recognized thoroughfares so that the people affected have an easy indicator as to whether they are in one constituency or another. Too often boundaries are traced through a zigzagging of streets which make no real political sense.
On this occasion I believe that the Commissioners acted with practical wisdom. I notice as well that they have given reasons for their changes. 1 fought a long time to have reasons included in decisions. In fact, there is a Bill presently on the Order Paper which I filed in April, 1980. It goes even further since it recommends the disqualification of a report if the Commisioners fail to respond to the representations that are made and do not include the reasons for having made changes.
I trust that I will have the opportunity to debate that Bill and put it forward again so that it will be accepted. It imposes no additional burden on the Commissioners. Under the first two redistributions that I have been through, I must say that the Commissioners' reports were simply flat-footed statements as to changes. There were no reasons given for those changes. The burden was on members to raise the objections. The Commissioners were under no obligation to listen to any recommendations. Frankly, we have some terrible dogs' breakfasts in many of the Provinces. It was so bad in one case after the 1971 redistribution, the proposals were so uniformly bad that, as one of my colleagues, who is no longer here, said, they had been gerrymandered by ignorance and incompetence.

And it costs a lot less and is a lot more effective than electing one more Member with everything that entails.
Mr. Speaker, since there are other Members who would like to speak, I merely wish to say that I urge the Government, my party Leader and the Leader of the New Democratic Party to agree to stop this redistribution, not because the Commission's work is unsatisfactory but for the very simple reason that we do not need redistribution at this time, unless perhaps to reduce the number of Members in this House. Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in the debate today on the question of electoral boundaries and how it will affect the Province of Alberta. As the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has already enunciated, the Commissioners have done an excellent job in their task. A number of Members of Parliament will be speaking on this subject. They will have some questions to put forward and some comments to make with regard to suggested changes they would like to see made, but the general feeling has been positive about the changes.
I am a Member of Parliament who represents a large, sprawling rural riding which at present contains 113 communities, villages and hamlets. My riding will become about 15 per cent larger. In spite of that, I welcome those new constituents. I feel privileged in representing a rural constituency as opposed to an urban one. It is more in keeping with my intentions of knowing the people.
However, I seize this opportunity to put on the record virtually the same concerns that were expressed by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West. I believe the House has long passed the optimum time to ask the logical question: How big should this institution become? Surely it should not be the perspective that every ten years the numbers of Members of Parliament increase. Surely we should not follow that road, fast-tracking into history without ever asking the question: When do we stop having a bigger and bigger Parliament?
The Electoral Boundaries Commission did its task well. It was under the direction of Parliament. The Commission was told the number of seats it had to carve out of Canada. We must ask a fundamental question: Is there some purpose or meaning to having 282 Members in the House of Commons? If there is one person in the chair and one person standing and speaking, it means that there are 280 persons listening. Is Canada better served by this? In fact, if we consider that the Speaker is listening also, then one person is speaking and 281 are listening. Will we be better served as Canadians when we have a House with 310 Members, with one speaking and 309 listening? How can we expect to sell to Canadians the idea that there is some advantage to that?
It must be recognized that the present system was put in place when Members of Parliament travelled from the Prairies, from British Columbia and from the outreaches of Atlantic Canada to Ottawa by train, when campaigns were conducted on horses and buggies. Also it must be recognized that today we live in the era of electronics. I visited the office of a Senator in the United States. He was able to a type letter,
push a button on the typewriter and have it transmitted to Portland, Oregon, to be signed with his signature by a signing machine there. Thus, when someone wrote to him to complain about the post office, within two days they had received an answer indicating what kind of service he was trying to create. This type of technology can put out massive amounts of mail. We can provide extended use of telephone calls. We can virtually go anywhere in Canada within less than a day's time. We can reach the more populated areas in four hours to five hours. Most of central Canada can be reached in 80 minutes or 90 minutes. Surely the theory that the population of the House of Commons has to grow larger and larger does not make sense.
At this point I want to emphasize that as the House becomes larger and larger, the concept of Parliament becomes less and less. I say this because each of us who represents a constituency will be able to speak that much less and will be able to ask fewer questions. Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party will be able to present fewer petitions because there will be the same number of hours in a day and the same number of days in a week.

Well, the only way we will change that is to adopt the metric week, the ten-day week and the 100-hour day. If we increase the numbers of Members, then by the pure bureaucracy of Parliament itself we will guarantee that the House of Commons is run by the executive council or by Cabinet. But we want a parliamentary situation where the Crowfoots, the Bow Rivers and other constituencies across the country have input in the House of Commons. We do now want to have a situation similar to the one in our mother Parliament in Westminster which now has 600 Members of Parliament, some of whom scarcely have an opportunity to speak in a month's period of time. That system is not acceptable.
Moreover, there are optimum sizes for decision-making groups. Once you get beyond 200 or 300 persons involved in making a decision, you are long past the optimum size for the House of Commons. If we are going to make joint decisions, the size of the House of Commons must be compatible with the objects of decision-making. We should not in every census period continually increase the size of this House without ever pausing to ask the basic and fundamental questions as to the size of House we should have with regard to the purpose by which this House is to serve the people of Canada.
I submit to the Government House Leader that before we go through this exercise again, we should make a study of how large this Parliament ought to be. There should be a new fundamental principle by which we guide ourselves with regard to where we put the boundaries. The automatic presumption that we will grow larger without end and without ever asking the question as to whether the public of Canada will be better
May 27, 1983

served by having more Members would demonstrate that we as parliamentarians lack the skill to ask the fundamental questions in problem solving.
If there are to be more Members of Parliament, there will be less time for each to speak. We will have an executive council running this place. Backbenchers will simply rubber-stamp the decisions that are brought forth.
The question ought to be looked at in a number of ways. Perhaps Members representing densely populated constituencies could be granted a larger staff. Members in very large rural areas could be granted more money so that they could have more than one constituency office. Constituents would then have greater accessibility to their Member of Parliament. In this day and age with modern technology, just because the population of this country grows larger, it is not necessary that the House of Commons grow larger as well.
It would be wrong for us to move as Great Britain has moved. I fall the Members of Parliament in Westminster wanted to be in the House of Commons at the same time, there would not be room. We remember occasions such as when Ronald Reagan, the President of the United States, visited Canada, and another time during the constitutional debate when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was going to speak and answer questions being raised by the public and the Opposition Members. There was intense interest in those speeches because of the importance the nation attached to them. Every seat in this House of Commons on both occasions was occupied. How can duly elected Members of Parliament feel comfortable about the fact that if we want to go to the House of Commons to listen to a very important speech we may arrive a moment too late and the House of Commons would be full? That would be unacceptable.
More important is the question of what size is optimum for decision making. There is also the fear that as we grow larger and larger we will have more and more government by executive. The backbencher will become increasingly less important. There will be less and less time for Members to ask questions and make speeches. The power of the executive will grow and balloon and grow and balloon to the point where it will become all-powerful. Parliament will be virtually destroyed.

I recommend that the House of Commons embark-and I hope Government Members put this initiative forward-on a system which asks basic questions. First, how large should this place be? Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to put a few thoughts on the record today. I begin by saying how pleased I am with what has happened with the changes in boundaries as they affect my riding. In my case, there were absolutely no changes. That is a good way to start. I am pleased with my riding and I would like it to stay that way. I will do my best to keep it that way for a long time.
It is important, when you look at the part of the country I represent, that the riding stay the same. That is certainly the case in my area. It is unique. It is an area set aside unto itself, an area that geographically must stick together. To separate any community would be to take it out of that real, live, living part of that central riding and put it into an area in which it would not fit comfortably. I can refer to several areas such as Fort Vermilion and La Crete. If you pull those out of my riding, the only other riding in which they would fit would be the neighbouring riding of Athabasca. It could only be reached by air or by travelling a distance of some 600 miles from the riding of Athabasca. That was the situation many years ago when Athabasca was represented by Dr. Yewchuk. At that time he represented that part of my district. It must have been very difficult for him and the people he represented in terms of traditional communication.
We have the example as well of an Indian reserve in another riding that is part of a group of Indian bands which I represent. The Band's head office is in my riding, but this particular band is represented by the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields). I know that he represents them well and he is happy to represent them, but from time to time I have visited with the band-I visited recently with Chief Johnson-and we had quite a discussion because I am already working on many of the concerns that affect that band as they affect the other bands in my riding. We can see that there is a natural link there.
Going to the southern part of the riding there is the area of Valleyview and McLennan. There again a unique pocket exists that needs to be part of the Peace River district.
Both of the Members who have spoken today about this particular Bill have dealt with the concerns on both sides of the House about increasing the number of Members we seem to be heading toward. I certainly have some concern about that, but today I want to talk about the impact that riding boundary changes could have on northern Alberta.
When talking about the formation of a riding, several factors must be taken into account. The first factor is, of course, the geographical factor, and I have referred to that. Things like roads become very significant, because roads are

the line of transportation, the communication route that, ordinary people tend to use. Things like rivers and lakes and, of course, mountains become natural barriers and those barriers must be considered when making sure that various ridings work together and fit together.
Another factor to be taken into account is that of social concerns. Those concerns take in a whole variety of things, and include, for example, business trade. In the North, there are very defined business routes and many communities shop within other communities. They are all tied in very closely. I believe that must be considered when designing new ridings and new riding boundaries. Another concern that, although it may not be significant in some parts of Canada, certainly is significant in northern Alberta is the whole concept of sports. We tend to have natural boundaries within which we compete, whether they be hockey teams, baseball teams or various other sports such as curling or golfing. Those concerns too must be considered in terms of boundaries.
Still another concern is that of industry. In a large agricultural community where much of the shopping and much of the industry needs are found within a certain area, it is obvious that those areas should be brought together and related together.
A third factor to be taken into account is communications. Radio stations, newspapers, television, become very significant within a riding because areas that are close together tend to communicate within that specific area as is certainly the case in my riding. There are certain newspapers which are distributed within my riding and, therefore, to have a certain portion of that riding taken away would make it difficult both for the Member and for the people within that area to keep communications flowing on an ongoing basis.
Of course there is the fourth factor which must be taken into account, that of historical concerns. These include agricultural and business relationships, family relationships, traditional communications, and so on. The ethnic groups must be considered as well. There are various ethnic groups living in certain areas which want to be included in the same area in terms of the same representation in the House of Commons.
The last factor which I think must be taken into account is the future of the area. This is what I consider to be a really important factor regarding riding adjustments in the northern part of Alberta, because we in the North work together, have many dreams in common, and therefore there are many natural tendencies which make us want to work together as a unit. We want our future growth and development to be considered in the choosing of riding boundaries.
When talking about the northern part of Alberta, I think that one of the big concerns I have is that the new riding boundaries, as they are selected, would tend to create splinters or little segments coming away from the central boundaries around Edmonton rather than create ridings which are truly northern ridings. We, of course, want ridings which are made up of that particular geographical region of our part of the Province. We do not want a little piece taken from the North
and added to the South just to create a more balanced population, because we really want to see that we can all continue to be represented in much the same manner.
My riding is very much like the riding of my colleague, the Hon Member for Athabasca. We have similar concerns, similar worries, similar problems simply because we face similar conditions and similar circumstances. I am speaking particularly of the growth potential which exists in the north of Alberta. The agricultural sector is still trying to develop new land. I have mentioned this to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in terms of our concern about the provision of railways and rail services for some kind of assistance to get grain from some of the farms into the central elevators which are, in many cases, 120 miles away. That is one concern that we both have because that is a concern which is common to the northern part of Alberta.
Another concern is respecting oil and gas, because there are oil and gas deposits in my particular region and, as result of that, those concerns tend to be common to a large number of people in that particular area. Those concerns may not be the same concerns as those of people in the southern part of the region.
The third resource which is present in the north of Alberta is forestry. Again this is a very common interest which tends to bring that area together. Of course there are other resources such as the tar sands which we all hope will go ahead some day soon. They were going ahead rather well before implementation of the National Energy Program, and of course right now everything has slowed down a little bit and there are some concerns about that. The glass sands as well are present in my riding and they will be developed along the Peace River in the next little while. Things are starting to happen with regard to glass sands.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that all these resources are unique to the region of northern Alberta and therefore tend to make the interests of northern Albertans unique. Our relationships and communications are unique. As a result of that, we want to be certain that when there is another riding in the North, it is representative of those particular concerns. We do not want to see the people of northern Alberta become splinter groups.
There are many communities in northern Alberta which 1 think demonstrate what I am trying to point out. These communities include Edson, which is of course represented by the Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), Valleyview, White-court, all communities that tend to be areas that are based upon resources, whether they be agricultural or oil and gas. There is a sort of camaraderie that exists between those communities which, though they are fairly close to the City of Edmonton, relate very well to a community like High Level, which is very near the territorial border in the northern part of the riding of Peace River. There is a common thread that runs through them all and allows them to relate to communities like Fort McMurray and Boyle in Athabasca.
So I think that it is absolutely essential that in forming these new riding boundaries, these kinds of concerns be taken into consideration. Of course, as I mentioned in the early part of

my comments, I am very pleased because in the riding which I represent, that of Peace River, the boundaries have not been changed. That allow us some flexibility to make certain that the boundaries do reflect that uniqueness.
The reason I am speaking today is that the motion which has been put forward relates to the riding of Athabasca. I just want to read into the record the particular concerns which exist, and they fall under the fourth concern of this particular motion. One of the objections reads:

In establishing the boundaries of the electoral district of Athabasca the Commission failed to give adequate consideration to demographic factors and revised the boundaries between the ridings of Athabasca and Lakeland in such fashion as to cause the population of the riding of Athabasca to fall well below the provincial average and the population of the riding of lakeland to increase to a level well above the provincial average.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SALARIES OF LIEUTENANT GOVERNORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased at this time to introduce for second reading Bill C-160, an Act to amend the Salaries Act in respect of the Lieutenant Governors of the Provinces.
Lieutenant Governors are perhaps the least understood of constitutional officers in Canada. The fact of their appointment by the Governor in Council by instrument under the Great Seal of Canada, coupled with this Parliament's responsibility for their salaries, provides an impression that these are federal officials. They are, in fact, the Sovereign's representatives in the right of the Provinces, as much Her Majesty's representatives for all purposes of provincial Government as the Governor General himself is for purposes of Dominion Government.
As such, these officials play an integral role in the fabric of their individual Provinces. While the degree of financial and other support provided by the Provinces for these officers varies considerably, they have ensured that these officials have the means to maintain the dignity of their role as Her Majesty's representatives.
Our Constitution charges this Parliament with "fixing and providing" the salaries of Lieutenant Governors. The amendment tabled today will provide these distinguished officials with salary increases of 6 per cent effective January 1, 1982, and 5 per cent effective January 1, 1983. In addition, the amendment will provide for automatic annual adjustments,
beginning in 1984, based on the formula which is used to determine annual increases for federally appointed judges.
The need for this automatic adjustment provision becomes obvious in view of the salary history of Lieutenant Governors. Since Confederation, there have been but three formal adjustments to these salaries, in 1873, 1965 and 1975. In the past, during periods of low inflation, there was not the necessity to adjust salaries on a regular basis, and this pattern of substantial periods of time, between increases, was evident in all salaries fixed by federal statute, including those of Members of Parliament, Senators and judges. This House has in recent years moved to provide automatic adjustments to those other salaries, leaving Lieutenant Governors without such a mechanism.
There are those who will argue that we should be proposing today increases higher than those contained in this Bill, in recognition of the period since the last increase. However, bearing in mind the sacrifices being made by all Canadians as we unite in our efforts toward economic recovery, and the allowances and support provided by both the federal and provincial Governments toward the expenses of the office, I know that these leading Canadians will support the level of increase proposed by the Government, and this and their respective provincial Governments' continued commitment to economic growth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak in the House on what I like to call "ecumenical Friday". It seems that quite often we deal with matters on Friday afternoons in the House of Commons in a very sane and civilized way, with some agreements. That has not always been the case on some Fridays over the last little while, but today, I believe, is one of those "ecumenical" days.
In continuing the debate begun by my friend, the Government House Leader, on an Act to amend the Salaries Act respecting Lieutenant-Governors of Canada, let me begin by referring the House to the power source of the Lieutenant-Governors. I quote' the following from the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1975, at page 18:
May 27, 1983

For each Province there shall be an Officer, styled the Lieutenant-Governor, appointed by the Governor General in Council by Instrument under the Great Seal of Canada.
The Act then goes on to indicate that he holds office during the pleasure of the Governor General, and 1 quote:
-but any Lieutenant-Governor appointed after the Commencement of the First Session of the Parliament of Canada shall not be removeable within Five Years from his Appointment, except for Cause assigned-
In other words, when a Lieutenant-Governor is appointed, he takes on a particular and peculiar status in the hierarchy of Government. 1 believe the Government House Leader was right when he said in his remarks that there were some people in the country who did not understand the significance of the role of Lieutenant-Governor. I believe it is important that the House and the country understand that it is not an honorary position. It is a position the holders of which enjoy particular powers within the community.
I want to say at the outset that I believe that every Government, whether it has been Liberal or Conservative, over the course of the years has taken great pains to ensure that the person who holds that position of Lieutenant-Governor-and I hope to demonstrate this a little later in my speech-is a person of standing in the community, not just of standing in the social or economic sense, but in the sense of accomplishment. The history has been that most of the Lieutenant-Governors in the country are appointed at the end of a long career in some other occupation where they stood for something, and in their appointment they stand for something by the nature of the persons who have been appointed.
Having said that, let us consider what the office is. It is an office which combines the monarchical and federal principles in the government of the Canadian Provinces. As the chief executive officer in each Province, the Lieutenant Governor succeeded the pre-1867 colonial Governor in his office, if not in his person, and as such he is the representative of the Crown within the Province and for the purposes of the provincial Government.
The category of representative of the Crown has some interesting and important constitutional perimeters. I believe it is well when we are considering the salaries of the Lieutenant Governors of Canada that we understand just how far that power ranges.
In his capacity, a Lieutenant Governor possesses the formal powers necessary for the working of the Cabinet or parliamentary Government. Moreover, the Lieutenant Governor has broad discretionary powers which may on occasion be exercised and, indeed, have been exercised. He alone has the responsibility, whatever the circumstances, of finding a Minister who can form a Government. He must be consulted on the summoning and the prorogation of the legislature of each of the Provinces. He must agree to the dissolution of the legislature and the date of an election. He can question and discuss Government policy. He has the power to dismiss a Government for unlawful or unconstitutional actions. He can, in short, refuse to follow the avice of his Ministers if, in his opinion, the public interest requires it. These powers cannot be defined, and while their exercise has been and must necessarily
Salaries Act
be infrequent, their existence provides the ultimate safeguard of the Constitution.
In the past, Lieutenant Governors have felt it necessary to refuse dissolution, to decline to make appointments, and on five occasions have found it necessary to dismiss their Governments. The Lieutenant Governor is also an officer of the Government of Canada. He is appointed and paid by the federal Government. He is liable to its instructions and may be dismissed by the federal Government. Two Lieutenant Governors, in Quebec in 1879 and in British Columbia in 1900, have been dismissed. The Lieutenant Governor is appointed and holds office "during pleasure", but the normal term is for about five years. All expenses of the office other than the salary and a small expense are borne by the provincial Government.
I thought it wise, because there are some people who would wonder why we would be looking to the salaries of Lieutenant Governors in this period of time, to indicate to the House of Commons that it is not an office pro forma; it is an office of substantial constitutional powers and duties. Going back to my opening remarks, I would like to say that it is an office to which Governments have given some considerable attention concerning the people who would fill them. It is wise for the House to understand that the woman and the men who are Lieutenant Governors in Canada now are very fine people. The salary was not their attraction to the office but, rather, the prestige and honour of serving in public office. I think this is true for all of them.
First, I would like to speak of our own Lieutenant Governor in the Province of Ontario, the Hon. John B. Aird, a very distinguished lawyer, a Member of this Parliament in the sense that he was a member of the Senate at one time. He has garnered a host of honorary degrees. He stood for excellence and he now stands for public service. He has been a distinguished military man, a chancellor of a university, a high officer in his church and one who has always taken an interest in public affairs. He succeeded the honourable Pauline McGibbon, who was the first women to be Lieutenant Governor. 1 do not think there is anyone in the House who would not say that Pauline McGibbon distinguished herself on every occasion as one who understood the nature of the office and its duties. She has been ably succeeded by the Hon. John B. Aird, who has brought great enthusiasm to his office and its duties, which, to some of us, would seem very onerous indeed. I have been with him on occasion in his Province and 1 have watched him on other occasions. 1 think that his appointment was brilliant. He has carried himself in that office with the same distinction as he has fulfilled every task he has undertaken. I said that the Lieutenant Governor stands for something, and that is indeed true of John Aird. I congratulate the Government on its choice. It could have found no one better.
Then there is the Hon. Henry Pybus Bell-Irving of Vancouver, a person who has distinguished himself in business, in his

Members agree with me that the Lieutenant Governor is a person who brings something to the office and whose presence in the office enhances it.
Finally, I want to talk about the Lieutenant Governor of Manitoba. The Lieutenant Governor is the Hon. Pearl McGonigal who is the second woman in Canadian history to occupy a vice regal post in Canada. The first woman, the Hon. Pauline McGibbon, brought distinction to her Province, herself and her sex in the performance of her duties.
I am satisfied that not only has the beginning of her service indicated the same for the Hon. Pearl McGonigal, but her period of time in that office will indicate the completion of that prophecy. Her great distinction is that she has been described as a veteran civic politician and one who is engaged in public life at the grass roots. Some of us ought not to forget about the grass roots. She has carried out the duties of her office and will continue to do so with great distinction. Those duties are rigorous indeed when one sees her schedule.
I thought I should mention that because, when we talk about the salaries of these people, Members will be as shocked as I was when I opened this Bill to learn of the level of the present salary for people who fill that office and carry out those duties which are ceremonial and constitutional and require attention seven days a week, 12 months of the year. I hope the House also shares the feeling that the proposal for the very small increases in salary, approximately $38,000, is not only overdue but small by any standard and beyond criticism.
Therefore, I wish to inform the House that it is our intention to support this Bill and have it put through at all stages. A Bill such as this should have been introduced long ago. While I can understand why the Bill was not introduced at the time we dealt with judges' salaries some time ago, it was certainly as timely then as it is now. Indeed, it is overdue.
What is the duty of Parliament? Judges are a peculiar breed of Canadians. They have no one to speak for them amongst their numbers except privately. If they speak out publicly, whether it concerns salary or anything else, they are admonished. I believe that is quite right and proper since they are put in a special place and given special responsibilities. The Lieutenant Governors are in no different position in terms of their ability to speak out for themselves on public issues. The fact that the clientele under this Bill are mute by law and tradition puts a duty on this House to speak for them. We have a duty to protect them and make judgments with respect to
Salaries Act
proposals that are brought forward for salary increases or anything else.
What criteria should a government apply? Certainly the salaries paid, whether to judges or Lieutenant Governors, ought not to be the factor which attract men and women to those offices. I can assure you that the Lieutenant Governors' salary is not what would attract a potential candidate to that office. But neither should a salary be at a level which would deter someone from accepting a call to fill that position. Once the Government has completed all its requirements for making an apointment, it should not have to overcome that impediment.
If the Government of the day feels that that is sufficient, then I am not prepared to argue with it. I am not prepared to argue with it in principle. I think it meets the tests in the criteria which I have put forward which I believe apply to those who cannot speak for themselves.
I want to tell the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) that it is our intention to support this legislation. I think it is fair, reasonable and long overdue.

May 26, 1983-That, in accordance with Section 54 of Schedule 1 of an Act to enact the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, to amend the Federal Court Act and the Canada Evidence Act, and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, Chapter 111 of the Statutes of Canada for the present session of Parliament, this House approves the appointment of Inger Hansen, Q.C., as Information Commissioner.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before speaking to the motion before us today, I would like to say how pleased I am that we have been able to make time to debate this resolution, since the proclamation of the Access to Information Act is awaiting the appointment of Canada's Information Commissioner. Should the motion being discussed be approved here today, as I hope it will be, and soon in the other place, proclamation of the Access to Information Act can take place 30 days after the appointment has been made. This is the earliest possible date that allows time for the Information Commissioner to establish her office in preparation for the coming into force of the Act.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members already know, Section 54 of the Access to Information Act, passed last July by Parliament, provides for the appointment of an Information Commissioner by the Governor in Council, and I quote:
-after approval of the appointment by resolution of the Senate and House of Commons.
The Information Commissioner holds office during good behaviour for a term of seven years, but may be removed by
May 27, 1983

the Governor in Council at any time on address of the Senate and House of Commons.

The purpose of this motion is to comply with the requirements of the Access to Information Act in requesting approval of the House to the appointment of Miss Inger Hansen to this position under the Great Seal of Canada. I do not believe there is anyone here today who is not aware of the work that Ms. Hansen has already done, in her effective and untiring way, in her present position as the Privacy Commissioner under Part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act. However, a few biographical details may be helpful in the House in considering this motion.
Inger Hansen is a native of Denmark and a graduate of the University of British Columbia Law School. As a member of the B.C. Bar she spent eight years in the general practice of law in Vancouver. She came to Ottawa in 1969 as a lawyer with the Department of Justice attached to the Ministry of the Solicitor General. One of her primary responsibilities there was to review the Juvenile Delinquents Act and prepare a proposal to replace it. Some Hon. Members will no doubt recall her appearances before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in connection with this matter.
In 1973 the Department of Justice lost a good lawyer and the inmates of penitentiaries gained an outspoken and effective ombudsman when Miss Hansen became Canada's first correctional investigator. In this position Ms. Hansen gained her initial experience in the art of being an ombudsman, an art she has mastered so well. She took her ombudsman skills to the Canadian Human Rights Commission in 1977 when she was appointed a Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the first Privacy Commissioner under Part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Today Ms. Hansen has earned the right to call herself Canada's senior ombudsman, having been in the field for ten years. In addition, she has built a solid international reputation for herself and for Canada in the ombudsman and data production fields. Over the past several years she has been active in the International Ombudsman's Association as a member of its planning committee. She is also a very active member of the International Association of Data Commissioners. She has chaired two of the latter group's recent annual meetings: in 1980 when Ms. Hansen hosted the meeting in Ottawa and again, by special request of the conference, in London this past summer. In all, Inger Hansen legitimately lays claim to a vast national and international network of friends and associates.
I would also like to say personally how much I have admired the work of Ms. Hansen. I first met her when I was a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and she first began her work in Ottawa. Subsequently, as Chairman of that Committee and as Chairman of the Subcommittee on Penitentiaries, I had good reason to observe her work
Information Commissioner
closely in the last number of months. As the Minister responsible for the Canadian Human Rights Commission, I have also had many contacts with her. She has not only been unfailingly courteous but also unfailingly effective in the performance of her duties. I would add that in my 15 years in Ottawa she is one of the people in the Public Service of Canada I have come to admire the most.

With all her experience, Inger Hansen is the ideal person to take up this challenge and set another precedent as the first Information Commissioner in Canada. The role of Information Commissioner is, of course, that of an ombudsman and is closely related to that of the Privacy Commissioner. The Access to Information Act provides that any Canadian who has been denied access to a document he has requested under the Act, who has failed to obtain the requested document within the prescribed time or who feels the fees charged are excessive, may lodge a complaint with the Information Commissioner.
The Commissioner will have extensive powers of investigation which will allow him to look fully into the problem and try to find a solution. I believe that this will happen in most cases and that no longer being required to institute an action at law will save Canadians both time and money. It will always be possible to appeal to the Federal Court in those cases where the problem has not been solved.

Of course the Information Commissioner is an officer reporting directly to Parliament. Being entirely free of the executive, the Commissioner will be at liberty to recommend release of government information, criticize the actions of the executive taken under the Act, table her recommendations in Parliament and take government institutions to court herself to obtain the release of information.
The Office of the Information Commissioner, as part of a two-tiered review system under an access to information scheme, represents a uniquely Canadian approach which the Government feels will maximize the disclosure of information under the Act at a minimal cost to Canadians. I am pleased to be able to speak on behalf of the Government to the motion that Inger Hansen be appointed to this position. In my view she is the ideal person to ensure that the position is developed to achieve its full potential. Therefore, on this basis I recommend to the House the resolution that the nomination of Inger Hansen as Information Commissioner be approved.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have been asked today to sepak on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition with respect to this appointment and if the rules permit it-certainly our customs do-to say that I second the appointment of Ms. Inger Hansen, Q.C., as the Information Commissioner. I think the Government has made a good choice. It is important that the new ombudsman or Information Commissioner start her role, not just with the approval of the Government, but with the approval of all

May 27, 1983
Information Commissioner
Parties in the House of Commons to which she will report from time to time during her tenure in office.
We have come a long way in the quest for freedom of information in Canada. For many years Mr. Barry Mather, a Member of the New Democratic Party, and Mr. Ged Baldwin, a Member of the Progressive Conservative Party, advocated the whole approach to openness in government. It was with some reluctance that the present Government was brought to the position where, if it was not intellectually committeed to access of information or freedom of information, it at least had to become politically committed to it.
We had a long debate and a long committee hearing on Bill C-143. The Bill was a shade different from Bill C-15 which I had the honour to bring in during the period of the Conservative Government. It was the first Government Bill on freedom of information, at least at the federal level, in Canada. Nonetheless, Bill C-43 was a welcome addition to the Order Paper of the House of Commons and will now, I am pleased to hear, be proclaimed on July 1 or thereabouts. July 1 is the date thirty days more or less from today. That is an important landmark or benchmark in the legislative history and in the evolution of the operation of government in Canada.
I will speak for a few moments about how important is the job of Information Commissioner in terms of the change this legislation heralds for the work, role and functions of government and the Public Service. The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) spoke a few moments ago about the ombudsman aspect of the role. That is right. In that role quite often the Information Commissioner will be called upon to go to reluctant Departments or heads of Departments to urge them to comply with a request, to intervene and to guide Departments. From time to time that Information Commissioner upon request will have to say to the subject, "You are not entitled to that information; it falls within an exemption". From time to time the Commissioner will instigage legal action or take other administrative action, including reporting to Parliament on defaulters within Government in terms of looking to the provisions of the Act and abiding by the provisions of the Act.
One cannot predict where this will go. Indeed, my Party is committed to looking at Bill C-43 in order to see where the present Access to Information Act does not comply with the Freedom of Information Act which we brought in in 1979 and to make amendments thereto. It would be wise for the House to consider Bill C-15 as well as Bill C-43 for the future.
Ged Baldwin used to day that once you put your foot upon the path, you cannot withdraw it. Frankly, I regret that the Information Commissioner, and the courts if necessary, because of limitations in the Bill will not have a chance to look at confidences of the Queen's Privy Council to see whether they are indeed confidences of the Queen's Privy Council. She will now have the responsibility, as I see the Act, of looking at those things that are to be declared confidences, at least in historic terms to see whether those things styled confidence of
the Queen's Privy Council have not suddenly become confidence of the Queen's Privy Council as a matter of convenience to avoid release.
I say all of those things because I believe that while this is a very exciting age in terms of openness in Government, the Commissioner, graced as she is with education, background, training and knowledge to do the job, is not going to find the job to be an easy one. There are some who would advocate that she become a pro counsel, so to speak, become quite aggressive in terms of the public and in terms of her activities under the statute. I do not know which is the right role. I cannot guide anyone in that respect. Miss Hansen will have to make her own way, as she has done in other matters and has done so competently. It is important that she be in the role to get her office organized. I suggest at the outset there will be a number of organizations and groups testing the waters of freedom of information rather quickly. Whether that flood is a continuing one or will diminish is a matter of opinion.
I spoke earlier about the relationship of the public servant and the adjustments that will have to be made within the Public Service. Those adjustments will take a great deal of time. The Government has done some preparation internally. There are information officers now either in place or about to be put in place in every Department. The Privy Council has done a great job in getting this organized. Banks of information, exempt and otherwise, are available and are being added to. The highest technological aids will be or are being used with respect to the information available. All of those things are there.
What has to happen is a natural change from a Public Service, which in the British tradition was secretive, to a Public Service which in the new Canadian tradition of openness which this Bill and this appointment is the beginning of openness. It is going to be hard, it is going to be quite difficult, expeciaily for older public servants to make that adjustment. Gradually as time goes on and the Information Commissioner does her work and the information officers begin to work, I am confident that the Public Service will adjust to the change. Let no one think it will not be difficult at the beginning for that adjustment to be made. Indeed, we are plowing new ground with this appointment, certainly in terms of this statute.
I share with other Members of the House of Commons a concern that the costs for obtaining information from the Government might very well be excessive. As I understand it, we have heard no final word with respect to that matter. My friend from British Columbia brought an indication of that to the House. It would be nice if today there could be tabled in the House of Commons a list of the fees so that we would know how much it is going to cost and we can make judgments with respect to it. I gather that is not to be.
I certainly hope the costs revealed by my friend for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) will not turn out to be the final cost and that a leak in that sense will have the same effect as the leak did with the budget. At least that provided more money for some programs. Perhaps the leak found by my friend for Burnaby will cause some sober second thoughts in terms of costs. It is very important that it not be viewed as a project on a cost-
May 27, 1983

recovery basis. That would bar many Canadians from access to information to which they are entitled.
We will probably have some expressions of regret or approval when we see what the final costs are. I ask the Government not to deal in anything but the most open way, understanding the purpose of the statute, expecialy at the beginning so that Canadians can get used to it and not be barred by excessive costs in the production of information.
The reporting to Parliament is important. She becomes a servant of Parliament. She also becomes a very important instrument in the ultimate parliamentary review that will take place in a few years down the road in the operation of that statute.
I said at the beginning that I think her appointment is a good one and a sound one. On behalf of all my colleagues in this Party, I wish her well. I hope and I believe that she will bring to her office the same accomplishment and dedication to duty that she has brought to every public office she has held. I congratulate her. I warmly welcome her to the office and we all wish her well.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and support the resolution before the House and thus make it unanimous, representing the desire of Members of Parliament of all Parties in this House that the newly appointed Information Commissioner, Inger Hansen, conduct her activities with the full support of Parliament and not just the Government of the day.
I am pleased that this legislation is finally going to be proclaimed. As Members know, for some time we were promised the date of April 1. I now understand that the legislation will be proclaimed on or about July 1.
I might also say with respect to the previous speaker that certainly the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) had a great deal of responsibility for the fact that this legislation is before the House today. It was that Hon. Member, in his capacity as Government House Leader and President of the Privy Council, who brought Bill C-115 before the Justice Committee in 1979, of which I was a Member. I am convinced that had it not been for that initiative on the part of that Member and that Government, the Liberal Government would not be bringing forward freedom of information legislation in this Parliament today. All of us in this House and indeed the Canadian public owe a debt of gratitude to the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton.
We also owe a debt of gratitude to Ged Baldwin who was instrumental in bringing this matter before the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, as well as one of my predecessors in this House, Barry Mather, who for a number of years from the mid-sixties tabled a Private Members' Bill and urged the Government to move forward in this very important area. I note that while the legislation will be proclaimed on July 1, there is, unfortunately, still a built-in delay in the Bill. The Bill provides for a transition period which in some circumstances will mean that information in the hands of the Government will not be made
Information Commissioner
available until July 1, 1986, some three years after proclamation of the legislation.
The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton made reference to the question of bureaucratic barriers that might subvert the spirit of freedom of information legislation. In my view it is absolutely essential that this spirit not be subverted by either unwarranted delays in the availability of information or certainly not by excess costs. Sometime ago I released a document which was a draft regulation which, in my view, would have meant that the costs proposed for access to information would be most unreasonable and excessive.
This fundamental right of access to information in a democratic society would have been turned into a privilege for those who could afford it. The draft regulations would have restricted access considerably. There would have been an initial application fee of $10, photocopying charges of 25 cents per page, and charges for computer time of $2.50 per quarter hour, this in a time when records are becoming increasingly computerized.
I am hopeful that the Government will recognize the degree of opposition to this proposal, which would have turned access to information legislation into basically a revenue-generating device for the Government as opposed to a means for ensuring that the Government is held to account by the provision of information.
As Ralph Nader, one of the pioneers of access to information legislation in the United States, said:
A well informed citizenry is the lifeblood of democracy ... The democratic process cannot function adequately without timely information about the activities of Parliament. A person should have the right of reasonable access to all public information in the possession of governments-
I might note as well that both the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party supported an amendment to the Charter of Rights, the fundamental statement of principles and values in the country, which would have recognized that access to information and freedom of information should be included as one of those fundamental rights in a free and democratic society.
Both the Minister of Justice and the spokesperson on behalf of the Official Opposition have made reference to the distinguished record of Inger Hansen. I need not add much to their remarks. I might say that I was particularly impressed by her outspoken and independent performance as the first correctional investigator for Canada. Most recently she has served as Privacy Commissioner under Part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act. It has been argued by some that the profile she adopted in that particular role and the extent to which the public was perhaps not made aware of the role that she was playing and indeed their rights under that Act was something that perhaps should have been changed. I am somewhat sympathetic to the arguments of those who have suggested that that office should indeed have a high profile. It is one thing to have rights entrenched in statutes but it is quite

May 27, 1983
Information Commissioner
another thing for members of the public to be aware of those rights and to seek to enforce them.
I would hope, therefore, that as Information Commissioner Inger Hansen would, in pursuing her new responsibilities, in fact seek to make the public very much aware of her new role and of the powers of her office, and indeed of the responsibilities that she has as Information Commissioner. I would certainly strongly support any request that she would make before the Justice committee or any Committee that may be monitoring this legislation for a sufficient budget in order that there may be widespread knowledge and education of the rights of the public under the access to information legislation. In short, I believe that Miss Hansen should have a very high profile in this role, unlike the role which she played as Privacy Commissioner.
I am confident that now that Miss Hansen has had an opportunity to study very carefully the legislation, and I know that she followed with great diligence the progress of the Bill through the Justice Committee, she will recognize that there is still a good deal of work to be done. I know that in her testimony before that Committee she did not express any criticisms of the substance of the Bill, although certainly most other witnesses who appeared before the Committee did express some serious concerns about a number of elements of the Bill. But I am confident that Miss Hansen will indeed recognize that the weaknesses in the Bill must in fact be corrected. It is fortunate that there is provision within the legislation for an ongoing review process as well as a report back to Parliament at the end of three years for general review and recommendations with respect to strengthening of the Act.
I believe that Inger Hansen has a very important role to play in the review process. She must not hesitate to speak out with her respected and articulate voice so that she will be heard, and of course the fact that she reports to Parliament and not to the Government will enhance her possibilities of doing so.
I have mentioned weaknesses in the legislation. I draw to the attention of Parliament three of the major areas of concern which I know that Miss Hansen herself is aware of. One area is the sweeping nature of the exemptions within the legislation, whether it be references to federal-provincial exemptions or law enforcement and subversive or hostile activities. Another area of concern is the second-class nature of judicial review within the legislation when there should in fact be full de novo review on the merits, and once again I am hopeful that the Committee which examines this legislation will recognize that indeed the original proposals in this respect in Bill C-15 should have been adopted.
The final area of concern is that sweeping provision which was inserted at the last stages of Committee hearings which permits the Government essentially to stamp any document it wishes as a confidence of the Queen's Privy Council, and which contains no review procedure whatsoever to ensure that that discretion on the part of Cabinet will not be abused.
I signal those areas of concern because, of course, the Bill itself does contain a number of weaknesses; but fortunately there is the provision for review. I am confident that Inger Hansen will exercise her responsibilities with distinction and that indeed her outspoken and independent performance as correctional investigator will be repeated in the performance of her new and very significant role as Information Commissioner. 1 congratulate her on her appointment and 1 am looking forward to working closely with her in the review process of this legislation. I know that all Members of Parliament would join with me in commending her for her record of service to the people of Canada and in wishing her well in the future.
