speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
That, in accordance with Section 53 of Schedule II of an Act to enact the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, to amend the Federal Court Act and the Canada Evidence Act, and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, Chapter 111 of the Statutes of Canada for the present session of Parliament, this House approves the appointment of John W. Grace, Esquire, as Privacy Commissioner.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as with the motion to approve the appointment of the Information Commissioner which was discussed earlier this afternoon and just approved, I am pleased to be speaking to this motion today. Proclamation of the Privacy Act, an Act which will significantly extend the rights of individuals with respect to the protection of information about themselves held by the Government of Canada, awaits the appointment of the Privacy Commissioner. If the motion being discussed is approved here today and soon in the other place, the proclamation of the Privacy Act will occur 30 days after the appointment has been made, parallel with the proclamation of the Access to Information Act.

Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members already know, Section 53 of the Privacy Act, passed last July by Parliament, provides for the appointment of a Privacy Commissioner by the Governor in Council, and I quote:
-after approval of the appointment by resolution of the Senate and House of Commons.
The Privacy Commissioner holds office during good behaviour for a term of seven years, but may be removed by the Governor in Council at any time on address of the Senate and House of Commons.

The purpose of this motion, therefore, is to comply with the requirements of the Privacy Act and to request the approval of
May 27, 1983

the House for the appointment of Dr. Grace to this position under the Great Seal of Canada.
Although I think everyone who is here today is familiar with Dr. Grace, in particular through his work as Editor and later Editor-in-Chief of the Ottawa Journal, I would like to put on record a few biographical details about him which 1 hope will be helpful to us in considering this motion.
John Grace is a native of the Ottawa Valley. He was born in Ottawa in 1927 and obtained his early education here. After receiving his BA from St. Patrick's College in 1949, he pursued post-graduate studies in English literature in the United States. When he completed his doctorate at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, he was appointed to the Faculty of English Language and Literature at that University. Dr. Grace was, in fact, the first graduate of the University of Michigan to be hired back by the University in 17 years. This action speaks for itself as an indication of the high esteem in which he was held.
Canada was very fortunate in 1959 when John Grace decided to return to Ottawa to join the Ottawa Journal as an editorial writer and member of the editorial board. This was the beginning of his long association with that newspaper. He was named Associate Editor in 1962 and, since 1972, was responsible for the editorial policy of the Ottawa Journal. From June, 1978 until August, 1980, when the newspaper ceased publication, he held the position of The Journal's VicePresident and Editor-in-Chief.
Most Members of the House are aware of Dr. Grace's reputation as an independent-minded, outspoken editorial writer. Whether or not we always shared Dr. Grace's views on particular issues, 1 believe we would all agree that integrity was a key quality in his editorials.
His skills as an editorial writer were certainly recognized by his peers. His editorials won two National Newspaper Awards in 1975 and 1977 and one citation for merit in 1974. These awards are the most prestigious awards in Canadian journalism. Today, he acts as a judge for those awards, again an indication of the respect those in the newspaper profession continue to hold for him.
During the period of time he served at The Journal in Ottawa. Dr. Grace also lectured on a part-time basis in the graduate school of the University of Ottawa. He has been a radio and television commentator on public affairs and served as a member of the Canada Council for six years. John Grace is currently a member of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, having been appointed to that position in October, 1980.
The independence he has demonstrated in that position will serve Dr. Grace extremely well in the position of Privacy Commissioner. The Privacy Commissioner, like the Information Commissioner we discussed earlier this afternoon, will be an ombudsman. One of the key responsibilities of the Privacy Commissioner will be to investigate complaints from individuals with respect to denials of access to information about
Privacy Commissioner
themselves. In this role, the Commissioner will represent individuals in ensuring that Government institutions are persuaded to provide as much access to personal information as is possible.

However, the Privacy Commissioner will not deal only with complaints. He will act as the Government's guard dog with regard to the collection, retention, use, disclosure and disposal of personal information by Federal institutions. He is specifically responsible for monitoring the implementation of all rules relating to information contained in the Privacy Act in order to ensure compliance by federal institutions. The Privacy Commissioner will report to the federal institutions when he is convinced that these rules are not being followed and he may report such instances to Parliament.

The Privacy Commissioner has also been given the responsibility of overseeing the use of exempt banks. If he finds that personal information has been improperly included in an exempt bank, he can refer the issue to the Federal Court. If the Court agrees with him, it can order the information removed from the bank.
Thus, the role of the Privacy Commissioner is an extremely important one. Through him, Canadians will be able to ensure that information about them held by the Government of Canada is protected in accordance with the requirements of the Act.
I am pleased to be able to speak, on behalf of the Government, to Dr. Grace's appointment to this position, and to add my personal estimate of his merits. He is a man of integrity; a man who has proved he is willing to stand up for his principles and beliefs. In addition, John Grace's long and distinguished career in journalism and his involvement in community services reflect his keen respect for individual rights.
It is therefore with pleasure that I move that the nomination of John Grace as Privacy Commissioner be approved.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to be able to join the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. MacGuigan) in this resolution. In fact, if the Chair wished to call upon me afterwards in connection with the formalities that are necessary in this House of Commons, I would be delighted to second the nomination of Dr. Grace as the new Privacy Commissioner, the new ombudsman.
Dr. Grace is not a constituent of mine but I think any Member of the House would be honoured to call that gentleman his constituent. The Minister mentioned that he is a true son of the Ottawa Valley. I think he has taken from that rich heritage some of the important attributes of independence, judgment, good humour, goodwill and an ability to work hard, to work diligently and to work well.
There is not a word that the Minister of Justice has spoken about him with which I could disagree. During his membership

May 27, 1983
Privacy Commissioner
of the CRTC he has been become known as the great dissenter. He is the Oliver Wendell Holmes of the CRTC. Dissent is a difficult thing among colleagues but he has shown that independence of spirit and mind that enables him to do that. His role is important and is becoming more important all the time. With advances in technology it becomes less difficult for information to be spilled and put into the wrong hands, particularly personal information.
1 suspect that the Government looked over the field of available candidates and came to the conclusion, as I would if I were sitting in the seat of the Minister of Justice, that there is no one more able, no one better fitted by temperament, education and attitude, than Dr. John Grace to fulfil the role of Privacy Commissioner. This is really a pioneering role under this new statute.
The Government has chosen wisely and has chosen well. 1 commend the appointment to the House and urge that it be accepted today.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again 1 am pleased to join with the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) in supporting the resolution before the House naming John Grace Privacy Commissioner, with new and expanded powers under the Privacy Act passed by Parliament some time ago.
I have not had the privilege of meeting John Grace personally but I have had conversations with him. In light of those conversations and my review of his record, I am confident that he will exhibit the independence and intellectual integrity so necessary to carry out this job with distinction.
I know of his record at the CRTC as a dissenter. I might say that on most of his dissents I profoundly disagree with him on the substance, but nevertheless the fact that he is not afraid to take a position which at times differs from that of his colleagues augurs well for his future independence in this important role of Privacy Commissioner. It is an essential role for a number of reasons. The Privacy Act which the Government has brought forward, in my view and in the view of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and a number of other commentators, is in many ways a sham. What has been proposed by a number of these individuals, and what in fact I moved in the committee examining this Bill, is that we should have separated the Privacy Act from the other provisions in the Bill because, far from being an Act which extends the protection of privacy of Canadians, it represents in a number of ways a sweeping attack on the privacy of Canadians. It grants broad new powers to heads of Government institutions, to the RCMP and to the new civilian Security Service to intrude into the most confidential and personal aspects of Canadians' lives. In many ways the Bill expands the powers which these agencies presently have.
I said that the Bill is in some sense a sham and I believe probably the best authority for that proposition would be the McDonald Commission itself which examined this legislation, having been tabled in the House during the time they were
considering changes in the area of security. The McDonald Commission was very critical of the proposed Privacy Act. They said, and I quote:
This legislative change goes too far in opening up access of confidential information to investigative bodies including the RCMP. ... the RCMP Security Service and the Criminal Investigations side of the Force have up until now been denied access to virtually all personal information possessed by other government institutions. (I emphasize legal access)
We all know the history of illegal access by the Security Service during, particularly, the 1970s. I quote again from the McDonald Commission:
The Commission refers to the "dangerously ambiguous reference" to the definition of "subversive or hostile activities" in both the freedom of information and privacy part of the bill.
Finally they say, and I quote once again:
-the proposed Privacy Act does not provide a satisfactory test or definition of the national security needs which may justify access to personal information in the government files. ... we think it is a mistake to provide statutory information for security intelligence gathering in such vague terms.
The McDonald Commission was absolutely right, Mr. Speaker. This Bill as drafted, the legislation which is shortly to be proclaimed, constitutes, as I have indicated, an attack on the privacy of Canadians and, certainly, not an extension of the protection of privacy of Canadians. In many ways the Bill is a misrepresentation.
The new Privacy Commissioner has his work cut out for him, certainly, but I am confident that John Grace will ably perform his mandate under this legislation. It is important to emphasize, as with the case of the Information Commissioner, that he reports not to the Government of the day but rather to Parliament itself. It is in recognition of that that this resolution is being brought before Parliament.
The provisions for ongoing review of the Bill are particularly significant in the case of the Privacy Act. Many of the most glaring inadequacies of this Bill I am confident John Grace himself will recognize quickly and will want to see changed.
I have referred to some of the criticisms of the McDonald Commission. As well, I would note that there are other weaknesses in the legislation which I would hope that Mr. Grace would be dealing with. There is no provision, for example, for the disclosure of the salaries of publicly appointed officials, whether it be the Northern Pipeline Commissioner, Mitchell Sharp, whether it be the head of the Canada Post Corporation, Michael Warren, or a number of others. These have remained hidden from public scrutiny.
As well, the legislation is totally inadequate in the manner in which it deals with the phenomenon of trans-border data flow. We see increasingly the flow across the Canadian border of confidential and sensitive data about the lives of Canadians, whether it be computerized data or other data. Once it has gotten into the data banks in the United States, for example, there is absolutely no guarantee, and there are no safeguards in this Bill, that the information in question will not be abused. The issue of Social Insurance Numbers and the potential abuse of Social Insurance Numbers was ignored in the Privacy Act and I would certainly hope that once again the new
May 27, 1983

Privacy Commissioner, Mr. Grace, would be addressing this question.
1 made reference in my comments with respect to the Information Commissioner to the importance of public awareness and education of the rights which they may have under this legislation. In view of my concern and the concern expressed by many commentators and, as I mentioned, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, this Bill does in fact represent a threat to the privacy of Canadians, taken particularly in conjunction with the new omnibus legislation tabled by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to create a civilian security service likely in 1984. It is essential, Mr. Speaker, for a person of the integrity, background and independence of mind of John Grace to bring his full powers to bear upon the Government and work very closely with the review committee to ensure that this fundamentally flawed piece of legislation will be significantly improved and amended following the review process. I hope that John Grace will not hesitate to speak out as the weaknesses in the legislation quickly become apparent.
I certainly hope as well that he will have an adequate budget to inform and educate Canadians as to his role as Privacy Commissioner, to make them aware of the rights which they may have under this new legislation, and the safeguards which exist in the Bill.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to join with Hon. Members of the House in agreeing to this resolution, and wish John Grace well in his very important and significant responsibilities over the next years in the interpretation and enforcement of the new privacy legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (for the Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983, BILL C-152 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-152, an Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see that we are back to the Fridays of old, and I appreciate the co-operation of Members on both sides of the House. I am particularly pleased with the major role being played in expediting the work of the House, and I may say it is most welcome, by the Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) with whom it has always been a pleasure and will continue to be a pleasure to work. I hope that
Government Organization Act, 1983 these preliminaries will not prevent the Bill from being passed before five o'clock, even if we do not have a firm agreement in this respect.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House today is basically proposing three things: a new Government structure in the areas of regional economic development, regional industrial expansion and external affairs, including international trade, as well as certain provisions relating to Parliamentary Secretaries, and finally, it also deals with the transitional provisions resulting from the proposed changes. Canada's economic and cultural resources are the result of both the diversity and the complementarity of its regions. This diversity and complementarity developed as a result of our history, the geography of our country, our political institutions, our cultural roots and our will to live together while respecting each other's differences. It is thanks to these immense human and material resources that we have developed so rapidly and that we are able to start our economic recovery with confidence.
National economic development that respects the regional differences in our country has always been one of the major concerns of the present Government. In the early 70's, we added to the then existing Government structure a department whose sole concern would be regional economic expansion. All Ministers who have been responsible for this Department have worked very hard to give Canadians in less developed regions a chance to realize the potential of their part of the country and thus contribute to the prosperity of all Canadians.
More than ten years later, Mr. Speaker, regional economic development has become so important that a single department can no longer meet the standards and objectives set by the Government. We therefore made a careful review of the administrative structures concerned with economic development and international trade, and we reached three main conclusions.
First, regional economic development could no longer be considered a specialized activity, restricted to the confines of a single department. It would now have to permeate all the Government's economic activities. Each sectorial department would, so to speak, have to be turned into a department of regional economic expansion for its own specific field. Thanks to DREE and to the efforts deployed by the Government, regional economic development had reached a level of maturity which made it necessary to integrate its objectives in the activities of all departments with an economic input.
Second, this redistribution of regional responsibility made it necessary to co-ordinate all Government efforts in this regard. It therefore became necessary to give regional economic considerations their proper place within the Government's central decision-making process.
Third, the close relationship between domestic economic growth and our international trade activities, the complexity of

May 27, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
the modern international environment, and the need for maximizing the use of Government resources allocated to international relations, made it necessary to reinforce Government structures in this area. It therefore became necessary to regroup our international trade resources and to integrate their activities in the general framework of international policy, while at the same time modernizing the institutions responsible for our international relations.
Mr. Speaker, it was therefore abundantly clear that the Government had to act quickly to acquire the structures needed to implement these recommendations. An in-depth review of the various structures involved was undertaken so that, in January 1982, the Government was in a position to announce its intention to revamp certain Government structures and introduce the present Bill into the House.
Part I of the Bill gives the Department of External Affairs a new organic act and highlights many respects of the evolution of the Department since the adoption of the Department of External Affairs Act in 1909.
The Bill brings together the responsibilities concerning international trade and the traditional activities of the Department with respect to external relations. Although it regroups the duties related to international trade within a distinct entity, the Bill acknowledges the need to stress their presence in our international relations as a whole. This Bill reflects the evolution and maturity of our diplomatic institutions. Ever since Canada gained recognition as an independent nation through the 1931 Statute of Westminster, it has distinguished itself on the international scene as a trade partner, an international system stabilizing agent, a host country for immigrants and refugees, and a dispenser of international development assistance. The interdependence of those various international roles and the complexity of the contemporary international environment have transformed the traditional diplomacy. The institutions proposed in this Bill reflect the conjunction of the various international activities required for coherently and efficiently representing the many Canadian interests. Hon. Members will note as well that, under the Bill, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be responsible for monitoring the Canadian International Development Agency.
Part II of the Bill creates the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion which will partly replace the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, thus bringing all industrial programs under the same roof. I would urge Hon. Members to read carefully that part of the Bill to realize the significance given to regional development. The regionalization of that new Department will be a model for all other sectorial Departments. The regional impact of all Government intervention processes will thus be heightened, and every effort will be made so that sectorial and regional considerations will indeed be taken into account in the preparation of our policies and the implementation of our programs.
Part III has to do with special areas and is aimed at deleting from the organic act of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion the provisions which concern special areas and which are now part and parcel of the Department of Regional Expansion Act. My colleague the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) will soon introduce in the House a Bill on the new regional industrial expansion program. He will need that Bill to carry out his new mandate, in addition to the tools which are already available.
Finally, Part IV introduces certain amendments to the Parliamentary Secretaries Act. It provides for the inclusion of Ministers in charge of ministries of state in figuring out the maximum number of MP's or senators who may be designated as Parliamentary Secretaries.
The fifth and last part of the Bill comprises a certain number of transitional provisions and amendments to the proclamation respecting the ministry of state for Economic Development. The proclamation spells out the new regional responsibilities of the Minister and proposes a new nomenclature to stress the importance of his role in the co-ordinating of regional economic development policies. The series of transitional provisions in that part of the Bill would indeed enable the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development to co-ordinate the overall regional economic development policy of the Government and would temporarily give the various sectorial Ministers the authority needed to assume their regional responsibilities in their respective areas. Under such provisions, those Ministers could, for instance, until the House approves the amendments required to the various statutes concerned, conclude sectorial agreements with Provinces under the new General Agreements on economic development that will be negotiated by the Minister of State on behalf of the Government.
The various Ministers whose portfolios are affected by these organizational changes will give details of how they were prepared and what improvements would ensue.
These changes essentially would guarantee a better management of regional economic development and increased benefits for all Canadians, wherever they may be. Moreover, they would enhance the importance of international trade within the overall context of our foreign relations. We will of course welcome any proposal that would improve the Bill as it now stands, but it is my hope that Members from both sides of the House will recognize the importance of expediting the Bill. It is in that spirit and to prevent any waste of time that I have so cursorily reviewed the contents of Bill C-152. It is my hope that in their comments, Hon. Members will show the same spirit of brevity and efficiency, and that the Bill go through all stages today, so that it may give effect to the reality of changes experienced in the organization of the Government over the last few months.
May 27, 1983

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1983, BILL C-152 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must disabuse the Government House Leader right at the beginning that the Bill will receive easy passage in the House of Commons, because it will not receive easy passage in the House of Commons. I do not want to put an end to the ecumenical nature of the Friday afternoon, but ecumenicalism demands not only friendship but also honesty.
I must say to my friends opposite, that great phalanx sitting across from me, that it is not our intention to give easy passage to the Bill because I believe there is something fundamentally wrong here. I suggest that this is organization and reorganization gone mad. The "locomotive engineer" behind this Bill has now left the Public Service; he rests in the other place. I believe Hon. Members know who I mean but I will be more specific: he is Michael Pitfield.
I was in the Parliamentary Library reading about Government organization and 1 came upon a statement by Edmund Burke written in 1791 which I believe everyone should keep in mind as we consider this latest animal from a Government that has gone mad in terms of reorganization. Edmund Burke said:
An ignorant man, who is not fool enough to meddle with his clock, is, however, sufficiently confident to think he can safely take to pieces and put together, at his pleasure, a moral machine of another guise, importance and complexity, composed of far other wheels and springs and balances and counteracting and cooperating powers. Men little think how immorally they act in rashly meddling with what they do not understand.
That is what this Bill is. It represents the little fingers of Government meddling around in Departments and agencies of the Government which were already doing their job quite well. There is a resentment within both the Department of External Affairs and the old Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce over the intent of this Bill.
This paper goes on further to say:
The urge to reorganize functions, authorities and relationships is evidently one of the most fundamental drives of senior public servants. If one thinks of organization structures as skeletal arrangements, then we suffer from a surfeit of radical chiropractors, who believe that manipulating the bones will somehow cause the organic diseases to disappear.
That is what this manipulative statute reminds me of. It goes on to say:
Second to this urge to reorganize is an urge to add on new layers of management, either under central agencies or within departments. If management is perceived as poor, we simply add more of it until the swamp is so full of swamp-drainers that managers have neither the time nor the clean line of sight for shooting the alligators.
Then it makes a plea:
There is a need then for a return to simplicity, clarity and speed of decisionmaking in the arrangement of functions and authorities, and a willingness to forego the highly-ornamental refinements that have given a rococo cast to our organization designs.
That describes to a tee what this Bill is intending to do to two fine Government Departments. Each of those Departments is designed for a specific purpose in the scheme of things and such is not only understood within Canada but abroad.
Government Organization Act, 1983
Let me quote from an article written by Jim Robb of the Ottawa Citizen. Under the byline it says:
Ed Lumley admits it.
The once lordly department of industry, trade and commerce, now the department of regional industrial expansion, has fallen in the government pecking order.
It has and that is what he says. It goes on:
"Industry, trade and commerce was Central Canada and manufacturing oriented, that's why it lost clout in the cabinet," Lumley said.
With high unemployment in the country and a necessity for upgrading our manufacturing sector in Canada for the good of its workers, the country and the world for that matter, I do not believe any Minister of the Crown ought to say that it has lost its clout. If it has lost its clout, as they say, do not blame the people in the Department and commence to reorganize it. I suggest a better solution is to strengthen the Department.
I have talked to people in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce who tell me that what has happened to that Department as a result of the intent of this statute has not been to strengthen or augment its powers and increase its scope, but to narrow it, downgrade it and render it ineffective. It has been to render it ineffective in the important sense that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was the route through which business came to Government. The managers, middle managers and upper managers in that Department understood their role. It was to be the touchstone of those industries to Government and a window of Government in the world in which those people move.
That purpose has been weakened and set aside. That is the wrong step to take in a period of reconstruction. It is equally wrong because Industry, Trade and Commerce had an external aspect to it. Furthermore, it is wrong for those people in the Department to be brought down and to intermingle with those who have a diplomatic and political role to play in the world abroad at a time when we require as much world trade as possible.
I want to say at the outset that there are no grounds upon which it could be reasonably argued that this Bill should have easy passage. While the Government has a majority and the Bill will eventually pass if the Government persists, I would rather that the Government would not persist. Instead, I would like to see the Government withdraw the Bill and reconsider it. I know it may be difficult for the Ministers of State to recreate it but it would not mean the end of the world.
I do not believe this reorganization is good either for the Department of External Affairs or the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the people who work in those Departments. That is why there is resistance which has caused difficulties and the delayed timetable. The reorganization has been a mess. The facts should be told as they are.
The second aspect of the Bill which I want to deal with concerns Parliamentary Secretaries. 1 want everyone in the House to know that suddenly it is the intention of the Government that Senators will be eligible to become Parliamentary Secretaries. I particularly draw this to the attention of that row of Private Members on the Government side who chaff to

Government Organization Act, 1983
get into the Cabinet in the dying days of the Government. Is it not wonderful that Senators can now be eligible to become Parliamentary Secretaries?

In the meantime the Government has decided that it will create Senators as Parliamentary Secretaries. Furthermore, it will increase the number of Parliamentary Secretaries by four. I suggest not.
I would like to find the person who dreamed up this idea. I would like to find him and have a chat with him. You are pointing to someone, Mr. Speaker, but I do not know to whom. If you have secret information on this subject, perhaps you would tell me afterwards, because I would be interested to know.
In any event, to put Parliamentary Secretaries in the Senate not only downgrades my colleagues on the other side of this House, but it tends to downgrade Parliament. It is not necessary to have attention paid to Parliamentary Secretaries. That Department was a signal to regions of the country that the Government of Canada cares, that it cares for disparities that exist in the country. Disparities have changed from place to place and from degree to degree, but disparities existed in Canada long before Confederation, at Confederation and up until today. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was the beacon light to the people and the regions of Canada that regional disparities would be cared for and were important. Lest you think I am being partisan about this, Mr. Speaker, let me assure you that I am not. The long and short of the 1982 reorganization-
This Bill is a result of that reorganization.

As for the new approach to working with the Provinces, implicit in the January, 1982 statement, we have serious concerns.
You can read the report, Mr. Spekaer; I do not want to take up that much time putting it all on the record. But again let

me point out the Senate report says "We have serious concerns". Under the previous structure, the least developed regions had a defender within the federal Government-the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this Bill and I will not speak at any great length. In essence, we are putting into law what is already in practice. I want to speak about that, in addition to the substance of the Bill. It is a bad practice to precede the enactment of the law in most instances, and I believe it to be bad in this instance as well. I do not agree with putting into practice or putting into force provisions of any law which has not received the approval of Parlliament. I suggest to the Government, just from that point of view alone, that it should be very cautious about that kind of procedure.
I have raised this objection on a number of different occasions as it applied to such things as the application of taxes and the collection of taxes where by precedent the Government assumed the right to impose that which it believed would become law at some subsequent date. In the process the

May 27, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
Government has been able to dip into the pockets of people- and in this case too in an indirect way-to extract moneys which they can ill afford in advance of any legislative approval. In this Bill similar things have happened. I want to register my strongest objection to that.
1 hope that this is a practice which will cease, that we will no longer be required to deal some months and in some instances years after the fact with proposals that the Government has deemed to be of value from its perspective but have not yet been given either the benefit of debate or approval by the House of Commons.
On the substance of the Bill, I have grave reservations about what the Government has done. I am vitally concerned about the effects of putting together two quite different functions of Government. I do not think that External Affairs and International Trade necessarily knit together under all circumstances. In fact, one can very frequently be an impediment to the good operation of the other. I also believe that each is of vital importance in its own right and should stand separately in the organization of Government. I believe that each has a priority position within the affairs of a nation, particularly this nation, a nation that sees itself in a middle role in international affairs seeking out compromise in a major dispute and attempting to influence the course of events, not as a major power but as a middle power.
For this country international affairs are of vital importance. I am always concerned when we are faced with matters of significant international import and we see the Government drawing back from making tough decisions about our relations with another country at the international and ambassadorial levels. I am always concerned when I see the Government drawing back because of the implications the decision might have on our trade arrangements.
Even separating the two functions may not totally eliminate that problem, but putting them together certainly compounds the problem. There are times when international relations or relations between countries are strained for one reason or another, but long established trade continues. To put the two together under one operation makes it very difficult to carry on those two vitally important functions without a very serious overlap. In looking at this Bill I must think that for whatever reasons-and I have tried to think of the reasons the Government has in mind-the Government decided to go ahead with this, it cannot be as compelling as the reasons for not doing it.
For example, we have had strained relations of late with Poland over the imposition of martial law and the inability of the communist Government there to deal in a way that we think would be proper with the people of that country and their right to free collective bargaining and free association. We have felt that we wanted to indicate to that regime that we were not favourable to what it was doing, that we were displeased and that we did not think it was an appropriate step to take.
On the other hand, Poland is one of our major trade partners, particularly for western grain. Because of this difference
in international relations we have seen a loss of the market for grain. The question one must ask is, who was hurt in that? Did we hurt the Government of Poland? Not very much because the European Common Market quickly filled the void in terms of the grain it wanted to purchase. Did we hurt the people of Poland? Not very much because, as I said, the European Common Market filled the void created as a result of our action. Well, whom did we hurt? We hurt the farmers of western Canada. We reduced the potential for sales.
In doing that, and some people might agree that is the appropriate thing to do, 1 predict the time will come when we will once again have normal relations with Poland at the international and diplomatic level. However, the chances of reestablishing the market for western grain will have been severely impeded, if not done away with entirely. I use the example to show the conflict. On the one hand, we have a diplomatic conflict, a conflict over the actions of another Government, an action that we absolutely abhor and want to see stopped. On the other hand we have an ongoing relationship at the trade level. What we have seen happen is that the people who in the end suffered from our actions were ourselves.
This is not the only example; there are other examples that have occurred over the years. I am not making a plea for change. I am suggesting that these matters have to be looked at singly. They cannot be looked at in tandem. I am concerned that by lumping trade in with External Affairs, the decisions that are going to be made about our trade arrangements will be very much determined by our attitude at the time at the international level with regard to our sense of the appropriateness of actions taken by one Government or another which may or may not be there for a long or short time, who knows.
Therefore, we will be detrimentally affecting our capacity to grow, to meet our needs, our capacity to provide opportunities for those who work in Canada and provide job opportunities for others. We will have detrimentally affected that as a result of lumping together these two vitally important issues.
For the foreseeable future, this country will depend to a great extent for its growth and economic future in terms of job creation, flow of finances and our ability to trade. Trade being a vital part of the Canadian way of life, it is very important that we should have a trade Minister, full status, dealing on behalf of Canada with the support of a Ministry that is capable of going out and, in a single-minded way, trying to improve the trade relations that Canada has to have in the future.
That does not mean that from time to time Governments may, for one reason or another, decide that the actions taking place in another part of the world are of such an important and reprehensible nature that we do not want to have anything to do with that country at all. Of course, there will be times like that. On those occasions the Government will make a political decision. That political decision will be transmitted from the
May 27, 1983

Government to the House of Commons, from the House of Commons to the people of Canada and from the people of Canada ultimately throughout the world that we are in the midst of a serious dispute with another country, that even to the level of trade we are prepared to enter into some kind of embargo arrangement, some kind of withdrawal of normal relations.
I suggest that under normal circumstances in international conflicts that likely will not arise. If it is our hope that we will build this country so that we will be able to provide for the needs for this generation and generations to come. If we are going fully to utilize the resource potential of this country, if we are going to take that and turn it into a manufacturing sector that will provide stability for people, if we are going to be able to say to those who have long been the backbone of our trading, farmers mostly in western Canada but not necessarily all, that there will be some conscientious effort put out by this Government through an agency or, I suggest, a Ministry, to try to build on what we are able to do well and create an image outside of Canada that countries can rely on Canada for providing certain goods and services that we are able to produce through our expertise and provide in a competitive way, then we need to have a single entity charged with the primary responsibility of trading. We must have a Minister in charge of a Department that is solely and completely directed toward the sale of Canadian products and trading with other countries of the world.
In my judgment, this is going in the wrong direction. If this were an attempt to streamline Government, if we could see Government trying to cut costs, make itself more efficient, provide for a more aggressive kind of external effort on the trade front while establishing an independent foreign policy-[DOT] although I do not know how-I concede that I might be persuaded that this could be done. However, this is not the purpose. As the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) pointed out, what we are doing is enlarging the size of the Government simultaneously with amalgamating two vitally important functions.
I have extremely grave doubts about the appropriateness of the direction the Government is going in this regard. I predict that within ten years this super Ministry will be split in two. The Government will see that it is too cumbersome, too difficult to operate in this way, that the conflicts are too many to resolve properly, that the decisions that must be made by the Minister who is primarily in charge come into conflict too often to allow decisions to be made properly, and will within the next ten years revert to separate operations, one dealing with external affairs and one dealing with trade.
In saying that, I do not propose that when that happens it automatically becomes once again the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I thought that Industry, Trade and Commerce was much too large. It covered too many conflicting interests. For a country like ours, there has to be a recognition that industry and commerce seen as a domestic matter are to be separated and dealt with in a separate way from our trade effort around the world. I do not suggest for a moment
Government Organization Act, 1983
that they are not interrelated, that there is not an overlapping of concern and operation, because there is. On the one hand you have to focus on what we have to do in order to build in Canada an infrastructure that will provide for our domestic needs, which quite clearly are our primary responsibility, and for our international requirements which are a great source of revenue to us and of great benefit to many other countries.
I suggest that that can only be done if the Government becomes somewhat single-minded about the need to encourage economic development on a world scale in Canada, economic development that recognizes the three frontiers which are open to us now in terms of trading, these being the Pacific rim, the United States and the European frontiers. There is the opportunity to move into those areas as they become somewhat more vulnerable and also to recognize the entire southern hemisphere. Over the years we will want to develop a good relationship with the southern hemisphere both in terms of our external operations at the diplomatic level and in terms of our trading arrangements, to our own benefit and to the benefit of the developing nations.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that all of those things can be accomplished by lumping everything together under one Minister. I do not think that anyone in the Cabinet could handle that, and not for one minute am I suggesting that Cabinet Ministers are less than competent, although I may have doubts about the odd one. I will not say which one because he is in the House. Nevertheless, I would say the same thing regardless of who I was speaking of. I would say it if my own colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), who I think would probably make an excellent Cabinet Minister and no doubt will when we form the Government after the next election, was the one to take on that responsibility. But I would even say to him with his infinite capacity which we all recognize, a capacity which is probably not even touched by anyone else in the House, that not even he could take on that much responsibility and do the job well.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, you can gather that I am not over-eager to approve this Bill. I am not really keen to put into law what I consider to be an inadequate piece of legislation dealing with matters that I frankly think are headed in the wrong direction. I do not think that the Bill would be a bad idea if there was some honest committee consideration of the whole question, and I stress honest. I think there is a need for Members to listen to each other as we try to explain why we are worried about the Bill. It is not a question of Liberals versus Tories versus NDP or, as is normally the case, Liberals and Tories versus NDP. This is a not a case like that at all. This is a case of being concerned about the future of the country, about what is actually best for the country. This is not a Liberal idea. It is not a Conservative idea. It is a wrong idea. These three things are frequently one and the same, but in this instance it is a wrong idea that we frankly must try to come to grips with.

I am addressing myself primarily to the question of the reorganization of the two Ministries. I recognize that there are other matters, but I am addressing myself primarily to that. The subject matter should be referred to committee and looked at in the most non-partisan way possible. It should be looked at from the point of view of how will it serve the various regions of Canada; how will conflicts arise between the two different functions; how will the one function be able to operate when a conflict is clearly there in the other function; how will it be able to maintain the equilibrium necessary between our country and another country when there is a serious conflict arising that is at the diplomatic level while there is the desire to maintain trade relations at the other level. How would we resolve those things within one Ministry? How could we make sure that both points of view are adequately expressed at Cabinet by people of similar rank? How would we give voice to the concerns within the Cabinet so that the Cabinet will be able to deal properly with concerns that may well be different but are of equal status?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the start, I wish that we had had an opportunity to debate this Bill before it became a fait accompli since I am convinced that it will ultimately be changed anyway. Let us not ram the thing through and then find ourselves in a position of rewriting the law again, and debating again because on the next occasion we may find that the Conservatives are on the other side of the argument, who knows. Let us not do it that way.
Let us see if maybe the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) might consider referring at least that portion of the Bill that I am concerned with to one or other of the standing committees or maybe even setting up a committee to deal with it by itself so as to see whether or not the conflicts that I envisage are real or imaginary. I will abide by the ultimate decision of the committee, as I must, and I will do it willingly. But let us at least give this a fair hearing and try to do what in the final analysis we believe is best. If we do not do so, then we will end up in the position we have found ourselves in so often in the past of having to come back and make amendments to something that everyone knew was not adequate enough to be passed at the time it was before us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) and he expressed some serious concerns which are well justified. I was rather amused by his fulsome praise of the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I gathered that he is getting in early with his support for one of the leadership candidates for the New Democratic Party in British Columbia. Why the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway would want to become the captain of that small Titanic is beyond me, but he appears to want it and he is getting his cheering section going early.
The Bill begins as follows:
Bill C-152, an Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto-
I think that part is well worded. "Matters related or incidental thereto" could mean anything that could be thought up and amended. I agree entirely with the Member for Hamilton Mountain who said that this is the wrong time for the Bill to come in. It is coming in in the middle of a process that presumably was to have had quite some time to go or else should never have been started. The amalgamation of the two Departments did get started in 1982, and now they are in a terrible shambles and want a Bill apparently to authorize the mess that they have made of it so far.
I think that they might better have taken some kind of initiative a year or so ago, brought out a white paper or a green paper saying that they planned to reorganize these two Departments and meld them into one Department, and then let it go to a committee to be studied so that there could be some warning given and possibly soem suggestions made by practical people. From reading the Bill, one cannot determine that there was any practicality at all in the genesis of this Bill. It looks very much like the product of a seventeenth century renaissance man's theorizing. I certainly agree with my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that the renaissance man with probably no sense of practicality whatsoever has decided that these two disparate Departments should work as one.
None of Canada's major trading partners has so far combined their departments of trade and foreign affairs. No other country thinks it will work. The last time something like this happened was about 15 years ago when it was decided not to integrate the Canadian Armed Forces but to unify them. About two years from now I expect they will be back where they were before this ill-conceived experiment started. I believe that if we go ahead with this ill-considered Bill we are going to have to do the same thing with External Affairs and Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Everybody knows that these Departments have to work together and there must be some integration of their activities. It would be nonsense if the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce sent a trade mission to Moscow to try to sell 10,000 refrigerators or something like that and at the same time the Department of External Affairs decided to break off trade relations with Moscow. I do not suppose there is a likelihood of such things happening but it shows the kind of integration that is needed.
When the Government saw the requirement its answer was: "Let's mash them together like potatoes and carrots and see if anyone likes it when it comes out". As far as I can see, no one does.
New positions have been imposed on a very rigid and fairly well working structure in the Department of External Affairs. I might say that I have always had a great admiration for the staff in the Department of External Affairs. It has had a long
May 27, 1983

succession of nonentities as Ministers, with one glowing exception in 1979 when the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was Minister. Other than that they have unfortunately had to take second-rank Ministers because the Prime Minister (Mr.Trudeau) wanted to run the place himself. It is much easier to do that if someone without too much intellectual muscle is the figurehead.
These people were put together by a kind of fiat in 1982, and suddenly 200 extra people had to be accommodated in the Pearson Building. Since then it seems they have just let them have a kind of group love-in until everyone found a place or what they might be able to or wanted to do. In other words, you kind of found your coffee mate there and decided between the two of you which department, section, division or subsection you wanted to work in. Then you tried to make a job description suit what you wanted to do. This has been going on ever since this ill-conceived idea came into full force.
It seems that we need some authority for the creation of all this confusion and that is why we have this Bill. I feel very certain that the Government does not really know what the Department will look like a year from now.
The effect of these changes so far is that the Department of External Affairs now has three Ministers. Presumably the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), that prescient Minister, is going to be in charge. When he was funding Alastair Gillespie's project in his constituency he did not know who Alastair Gillespie was, despite the fact that they had served together in Cabinet for years.
The other Minister will be the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), I presume, although what he is supposed to do is questionable unless it is to act as a kind of batman for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Then there is the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Lapointe), who has a questionable job as well. I do not know why we need a Minister of State for External Relations and a Secretary of State for External Affairs. Perhaps this will enable them to continue their travelling; one will be away and one will be at home-a kind of tag team wrestling match in the diplomatic field. This entire shuffle seems to be similar to a game of musical chairs. They were one chair short and someone was going to be left out if they did not dream up a job for them. Now they have it.

I do not think anyone should rejoice about that because that $61,600 is not going to be saved. Below that appears an amendment to add "The Minister of Regional and Industrial

Expansion $30,800, The Minister of International Trade $30,800 and the Minister for External Relations $30,800". This seems to me to be $30,800 more than was cancelled.
Perhaps someone on the Government side might be kind enough to explain in the days or weeks ahead whether we are going to spend an extra $30,800 on an extra Minister as well as the four extra Parliamentary Secretaries mentioned by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) a few minutes ago. I support what he said. It seems ridiculous to think of a Parliamentary Secretary being in the Senate. We cannot even talk to the Ministers who are in the Senate but have to listen to some stooge in this House when we have a question that belongs over there. That they would have Parliamentary Secretaries help them be unavailable is difficult to contemplate.
The Minister of State for External Relations, in his unusual job, is responsible for francophone, cultural and humanitarian affairs. It is difficult to know what his place will be in all of this. Among the people who are selling things, he has a very narrow job description.
In addition to these Ministers there is a plethora of Deputy Ministers. There is one of whom I highly approve. There will be one Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, the deputy head of the Department. We all know that Mr. Masse is an excellent administrator. I can only feel sorry for him, being given this garbage to sort out.
There will also be three Associate Under-Secretaries of State for External Affairs with the rank of Department Deputy Minister. Bill C-152 provides that one may be appointed Deputy Minister for International Trade and one may be appointed Deputy Minister for Foreign Policy. That is two, so it is a little difficult to see why we need another one but we have another one.
Meanwhile, at the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce there are more problems. Parts of the Departments are going to merge and become the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. According to the job descriptions, one Minister will be in charge of manufacturing, processing and service industries within Canada, regional industrial development, tourism, small business, and trade and commerce within Canada. I do not know if this means we no longer need a Minister of Small Business and Tourism or not. The Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Romp-key), who is at present the Minister of Small Business and Tourism, seems to be looking for a role to play in all of this. I do not know whether he is going to find one or not. It is difficult to tell in this hodge-podge of a Bill.
One of the big concerns in the country among businessmen is that the new organization will effectively kill the trade commissioners and that service which used to answer directly to the Minister of State for International Trade under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Canadian businessmen are concerned that the officers of the Department

May 27, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
of External Affairs will be unable to maintain the close industry sector contacts which they had at Industry, Trade and Commerce. Just how much trade expertise are our foreign service officers expected to accrue? It is a very important question in light of the fact that the changes have been selected to give trade matters a much higher profile. The answer to that question will affect not only the way the foreign officers go about their jobs, but also their career progression. All these changes will, of course, have a substantial effect on Canada's policy. Unfortunately, no one seems to know what the effect will be.
In February of this year the Financial Post, in an article by a brilliant young journalist by the name of James Bagnall, summed up the changes this way, and I quote:
On paper, all of these changes had a certain elegant rationale. But in the short run, they have produced bureaucratic infighting over office space, line responsibility and policy mandates. In addition, they have badly damaged morale within I.T.C., stirred the resentment of the trade commissioner service, which prided itself on its independence, left at least 300 employees from various Departments in a non-man's land with no obvious place to hang their hats and will eliminate more than 400 full-time jobs by the time the dust settles.
The article went on to say, and I quote:
Trade officials are still concerned their impact on foreign policy will be diluted by the new arrangement-they are outnumbered by foreign service officers nearly three to one domestically and nearly two to one abroad.
The sad part of all of this is that this came about without any recognition being given to the McDougall Report which was, as Hon. Members know, a Royal Commission Report on External Affairs. It was commissioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), no less, who said at the time that he thought that the Department of External Affairs needed to be reorganized to give the people a clearer understanding of their role in the Department. This report was handed in and within six weeks after that this reorganization was put into effect, apparently without any recognition being given at all to the Royal Commission Report by Miss McDougall, a very highly regarded member of the Department of External Affairs for several years. She was, unfortunately, somewhat hindered by a degree of independence which caused her report not to fulfil the secret dreams and wishes of the Government. It simply made sense.
I would like to point out that I agree with my hon. colleague that this bears all the earmarks of the work of Senator Pitfield, the person who brought in the National Energy Program, where he collected a lot of people who knew nothing about energy and devised a program to help the poor industry out which was doing very, very well up until then. He has now decided to reorganize that Department, where his knowledge is equally scant. As I read about the reorganization, I kept thinking to myself that I have heard of these things before, but where was it? Where it was was in "Gulliver's Travels", written in the eighteenth century. It is about the third trip Gulliver made to a place called "Laputa". This was an island in the sky where everyone dreamed funny dreams which were very, very impractical. In the capital city of Lagado they had a
place called the "Grand Academy" where all of these impractical ideas everyone had were brought together and they tried to put them into production.
I would just like to read something which Mr. Pitfield could well have thought up himself. They had a department of agriculture in this Grand Academy, and someone decided that they should find a device for ploughing ground with hogs so they would save the charges of ploughs, cattle and labour. The medhod they came up with was this, and I quote:
-in an acre of ground you bury, at six inches distance and eight deep, a quantity of acorns, dates, chestnuts, and other mast or vegetables, whereof these animals are fondest; then you drive six hundred or more of them into the field, where, in a few days, they will root up the whole ground in search of their food and make it fit for sowing; it is true, upon experiment, they found the charge and trouble very great, and they had little or no crop. However, it is not doubted that this invention may be capable of great improvement.
So they were quite satisfied with the experiment and they went on for years trying to sow ground which they had ploughed in this fashion.
There was another idea at the Grand Academy which would do Mr. Pitfield very well. I sometimes wonder if he could not have been a resurrection from the days of Jonathan Swift. At the Grand Academy everyone knew how laborious the usual method was of attaining to arts and sciences, whereas they contrived that the most ignorant person, at a reasonable charge and with a little bodily labour, may write books on philosophy, poetry, politics, law, mathematics and theology, without the least assistance from genius or study. We have a lot of people in this country who want to be able to do great things, but they are not all that willing to study and are not in the genius field either. A professor at the Grand Academy showed Gulliver a frame he had built, about the sides whereof all his pupils stood in ranks, and I quote:
It was twenty feet square, placed in the middle of the room. The superficies were composed of several bits of wood, about the bigness of a die, but some larger than others. They were all linked together by slender wires. These bits of wood were covered on every square with paper pasted on them; and on these papers were written all the words of their language in their several moods, tenses, and declensions, but without any order. The professor then desired me to observe, for he was going to set his engine at work. The pupils at his command took each of them hold of an iron handle, whereof there were forty fixed round the edges of the frame: and, giving them a sudden turn, the whole disposition of the words was entirely changed. He then commanded six-and-thirty of the lads to read the several lines softly as the appeared upon the frame; and, where they found three or four words together that might make part of a sentence, they dictated to the four remaining boys who were scribes. This work was repeated three or four times, and at every turn the engine was so contrived that the words shifted into new places, as the square bits of wood moved upside down.
Six hours a day the young students were employed in this labour, and the professor showed me several volumes in large folio already collected of broken sentences, which he intended to piece together, and, out of those rich materials to give the world a complete body of all arts and sciences-
Of course, it did not work. He was an impractical man. He was the "Pitfield" of his day. Mix everything up and maybe something sensible will come out of it. It is like the dictionary which some soul wrote as the words came into his mind. He ended up with the world's only dictionary which was not in alphabetical order. It was a very good dictionrary but not very practical.
That is what this Bill is like, Mr. Speaker. They do not know what they are doing. The people are milling around in the Pearson Building and the Government seems to be hoping that

something good will come of it all, which would be just about as accidental as finding a word you are looking for in a dictionary which is not in alphabetical order.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) mentioned, towards the final part of his comments, the report of Miss McDougall. I believe we must go back to that particular report to understand the genesis of this Bill, or part of the Bill, and also to understand what is not in this Bill.
On December 15, 1981 the Report of the Royal Commission on Conditions in the Foreign Service was released. One of the most important comments in that release, Mr. Speaker, was in the second paragraph. It is most important as far as I was concerned, because, having served 25 years in the Department of External Affairs, I was aware of the problems which Miss McDougall was asked to consider in the course of her Royal Commission. The press release stated:
Miss McDougall stated that the problems in each of these areas were of sufficient scope and complexity to raise doubts about the capacity of the foreign service to continue to function effectively. It was the cumulative impact of these problems on the service that eroded morale, purpose and confidence-
That was a very penetrating comment about the Department of External Affairs as it existed during the seventies and on into the eighties. I am not sure, but presumably it was at the back of the mind of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he asked Miss McDougall to undertake the Royal Commission and to examine the conditions in the foreign service. I rather suspect that it was not in the Prime Minister's mind, as a matter of fact, although he did appoint the Royal Commission.
I would like to read one other section of her Report and then return to some of her recommendations because they have a bearing on the Bill which I will consider in a couple of minutes. On page 21 of her Report, which was made public on December 15, 1981, she states:
There is indeed a profound malaise in the foreign service-a malaise that if not met by decisive and early action may put in serious question the viability of the career rotational foreign service as we know it today.
The Report was released in December of 1981 and today we have before us a Bill which was given first reading on May 5 of this year, roughly 18 months later, which purports, I suppose one might say, to deal with this malaise. I can assure Your Honour before going any further that it will not do anything of the kind. It will increase the malaise, there is no question in my mind.
This particular Report outlined in very careful terms the problems confronted by the Department of External Affairs both here and abroad. Miss McDougall made a couple of even more succinct comments about the malaise, one of them being Recommendation 44, which states:
Government Organization Act, 1983
Concrete steps be taken to correct the widely held view that those in positions of power consider the activities and the product of the foreign service as largely irrelevant to federal Government or Canadian objectives.
That sentiment had its genesis upon the arrival, in the seat of the Prime Minister's office, of the current Prime Minister, because he determined that he should be running the foreign service regardless of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
As I say, these matters were made public on December 15, 1981. Within a month, almost four weeks to the day, the Prime Minister announced a major reorganization of the Department of External Affairs in terms which we now find more or less embodied in the Bill, in more or less legal language, language which I would hardly call legal; but I will return to that subject in due course.
The Prime Minister's statement in January of 1982 was in total disregard of the recommendations which were brought forward by Miss McDougall in her Report. I suggest that that, in itself, was enough to destroy any hopes that there might have been, which could have emerged from the Report of Miss McDougall. It is really distressing, when one comes to think of it, that a Royal Commission was appointed to examine the role of the foreign service officer and the problems of serving in the foreign service and then to find that within a month the Prime Minister came out with a completely different sort or organization. To my way of thinking, this merely carries out the sequence of the unsettling change and the transfer to which the Department of External Affairs has been subject since 1968.
If I may, I would simply like to list some of the changes which have been introduced into the Department of External Affairs since that time, over the last 15 years. I cannot list them in the exact chronological order, but I think it deserves to be said that no sooner had one of these particular changes started to take root and become assimilated and the personnel were not even becoming accustomed to these various changes, that lo, the next one was brought on top of the others.
One of the changes that I remember, even from when I was in the Department, concerned an examination of the organization of the Department by a managerial firm called Ulrich, Currie and its subsequent report. The main outflow from the report was that members of the firm, Ulrich, Currie, or those who were carrying out the examination of the Department in the name of that particular company, found niches for themselves in the Department of External Affairs and started the expansion of that particular Department. Granted, they were in the administrative field, but that, in itself, was enough to unsettle a number of members of the foreign service.
The next change was program budgeting. As I say, people were just becoming accustomed to one change and then another one came along. Program budgeting consisted of a course in business administration which was carried on by a number of hotshot managerial experts going about the country and in the Department of External Affairs, trying to reorganize the Department on the basis of the programs which the Department was carrying out. There was a great general shift

May 27, 1983
Government Organization Act, 1983
of desks in the Department at that particular time. The program was just about assimilated when along came the managing of the Department by committees. A committee structure was set up within the various programs and the Department was being organized and run by that sort of committee.
On top of all this, of course, came the bilingualism program. At that time one might call a colleague only to find that he was not there. He was not being replaced; he was off taking a course in either English or French. That, of itself, was certainly unsettling. This affected mature, professional people who had earned a place for themselves.
One of the most important criticism which one can make of the bilingualism program, then and now, is that there is being foisted upon mature, professional people, the necessity to undertake studies in an area where they feel they are not able
to meet the same professional standard they met when they were a little younger. It is folly to impose that on mature adults who, in any event, are involved in their professional expertise and doing the best that they can in those conditions. The absences from their desks, of course, was also a very serious criticism.
May I call it five o'clock at this point, Mr. Speaker? 1 have a good many more comments to make on the Bill.
